# nephew

> Your logged-in identity, in any agent sandbox. Portable · Continuous · Yours.

Nephew is the profile layer for the sandbox providers you already use. It
carries one logged-in browser identity — cookies, session state, a coherent
fingerprint, and a pinned egress IP — into Modal, Steel, Browser Use, and
Browserbase. It
is not another sandbox and does not replace them: jobs still run on the
user's provider, under the user's account. Nephew is the identity they run
as. There is no Nephew account to create and no Nephew cloud in the middle;
no Nephew server exists, and no server ever holds a profile.

## What the user brings

- Their own provider accounts and keys: a Modal token pair, a Steel API
  key, a Browser Use API key, a Browserbase API key. Nephew runs on the
  user's accounts; provider billing stays the user's.
- Their own Bright Data zone: the dedicated IP the identity egresses from,
  pinned in the profile recipe.
- Node.js 22 or newer on the machine running the CLI.
- Keys live on the user's machine only (environment variables and the
  user's own provider configs). Nephew never stores the user's keys.

## Install

curl -fsSL https://nephew.ai/install | sh

The installer writes exactly two things: the app to ~/.local/lib/nephew and
a launcher to ~/.local/bin/nephew. No sudo, nothing else. The download is
verified against the published SHA256SUMS
(https://nephew.ai/releases/SHA256SUMS) before anything is installed; a
mismatch aborts the install.

## Commands (the nephew CLI)

- nephew init — connect the user's own provider accounts
- nephew capture — sign in once, in the user's own browser; the session is
  sealed into an encrypted bundle the user holds
- nephew run <job> --provider modal|steel|browseruse|browserbase — run a
  job as the carried identity
- nephew run <job> --provider steel --handoff (also browseruse and
  browserbase) — if the run is challenged, hold the live session for a
  streamed human handoff
- nephew revoke — destroy a bundle and its key material; leaves an
  Ed25519-signed deletion receipt the user can verify independently
- nephew receipt verify <file> — verify a signed run receipt (PASS, or
  FAIL naming the field that changed)
- nephew mcp — MCP server exposing the profile_run tool

## How it works

1. Capture once. Sign in once; the session is sealed into an encrypted
   bundle the user holds — profile state, fingerprint recipe, pinned proxy
   reference. Keys never leave the user's machine.
2. Run anywhere. `nephew run` starts the provider sandbox, measures the
   live browser, and checks it against the recipe. The fingerprint gate
   must accept before any state is released — on mismatch, the run
   refuses. Every run opens with a three-line trust receipt: the profile,
   the fingerprint it must match, and the egress it must come from.
3. Challenged: live handoff. If a site challenges the run, it pauses with
   LOGIN_REQUIRED. On Steel, Browser Use, and Browserbase the run can
   hold its live session instead of closing it: the profile's designated human opens a
   local (loopback-only) page, watches the session stream live, and fixes
   the login in place with their own mouse and keyboard. Rules: one
   handoff at a time, one controller, a per-handoff token bound to the
   bundle's designated human, and a hard deadline (default 360 s) computed
   on a monotonic clock — late arrival, reloads, reconnects, and
   wall-clock changes cannot extend it. Hand control back (resume) and
   the fixed session is captured into the same bundle; end the run or let
   the deadline expire and nothing is captured. Modal cannot attach a
   live handoff yet: its browser runs inside the sandbox with no
   host-side session to lend, so a Modal run that needs a login returns
   the plain LOGIN_REQUIRED pause.
4. Capture back. When the job ends, the live session is sealed back into
   the same bundle. One identity, no forks — the next run, on any
   provider, continues where the last one stopped.

## Signed run receipts

A run leaves a signed record: profile, run, provider, the fingerprint
hashes it measured, the egress it observed, start and end times, the
outcome, how many minutes of human attention it took, and whether a
handoff was used. The receipt is signed with the user's own Ed25519 key —
the same key that signs the deletion receipt — and stored in
~/.nephew/receipts/. Anyone can verify it against the owner's public key
with `nephew receipt verify <file>`; verification returns PASS, or FAIL
naming the field that changed. A handoff writes its own event record of
counts and identifiers only (frames relayed, inputs forwarded, outcome) —
no frames, no keystrokes, no page content, no token.

## Surfaces

- CLI: init, capture, run, revoke, receipt verify
- MCP server: `nephew mcp`, tool `profile_run` — same fingerprint gate, a
  structured LOGIN_REQUIRED pause result, and on Steel, Browser Use, and
  Browserbase the live handoff handle routed with the pause
- TypeScript helper: `withProfile` wraps a job function in a carried
  identity — Steel, Browser Use, and Browserbase today; Modal runs
  through the CLI
- Python decorator: `with_profile` in the `nephew` Python package wraps a
  Python job function (or a `with` block) in the same carried identity —
  same gate, same signed run receipts; Steel, Browser Use, and
  Browserbase today; Modal runs through the CLI
- Help page: https://nephew.ai/help.html

## Compatibility

Today: Modal, Steel, Browser Use, Browserbase — the same bundle, the
same gate, all four. On Browserbase the bundle is the only state a
session sees: Nephew never uses Browserbase Contexts (their
provider-native persistent profiles), and sessions are created with
your API key alone — no project id, no stored profile on their side.

## Measured proof

- Same profile, the owner's machine vs a Modal sandbox: identical
  fingerprints — all 10 measured elements, canvas included — with the
  pinned font pack in both environments.
- Pinned egress, verified live: a Modal run egressed from the profile's
  own dedicated IP, exactly as pinned in its recipe. The gate checked the
  egress before releasing state and accepted, and the session was
  restored. The address itself is carried in the run's own metrics
  record; each run produces the same record for its own IP.
- Baseline restores: ~6.4 s on Steel, ~7.8 s on Browser Use, ~5.7 s on
  Browserbase; full Modal runs 10–27 s in-session.
- 0 login prompts, 0 MFA prompts across the Steel, Browser Use, Modal,
  and Browserbase proof runs.

## Plain limits

- A site can still challenge a run. When it does, the run pauses with
  LOGIN_REQUIRED; the live handoff is the recovery on Steel, Browser
  Use, and Browserbase, and on Modal the recovery is still re-capture
  and retry.
- Browserbase sessions: the 5-minute timeout shown in a project's
  settings is the default when no timeout is requested. Nephew requests
  an explicit session window (1 hour) — measured granted in full,
  including a probe at the 21,600-second API maximum.
- One dedicated IP per identity, per-profile by design.
- A handoff is one designated human, one controller, on a loopback page —
  and it ends at its deadline whether the login is fixed or not.
- No "works on every site" claims. The proof runs above are the runs
  actually measured; every run is measured the same way and writes its
  own metrics record.

## Pricing

You pay for profiles — identities you own and can revoke or take
elsewhere — and for run-hours, the time an agent spends logged in as you.
No per-seat fees.

- Free — $0: 2 profiles, BYO mode; 1 hosted run-hour trial; concurrency 1
- BYO — $19/mo: 10 profiles on your own Modal, Steel, Browser Use,
  Browserbase or Bright Data accounts; unlimited run-hours (you pay your
  providers directly); extra profiles $3/mo; concurrency 3
- Hosted — $59/mo: 5 profiles, each with its own dedicated ISP IP; 30
  run-hours included, then $0.60/run-hour; concurrency 3
- Hosted Team — $199/mo: 20 profiles with dedicated ISP IPs; 200
  run-hours included, then $0.50/run-hour; profile sharing, priority
  support; concurrency 10
- Enterprise — custom: unlimited profiles; own-stack / BYOC deploy, SSO,
  custom regions, SLA
